## The assignment {.unnumbered}

You are the genomics data scientist on a team that works on obesity. A project lead has noticed that the strongest common variant signal for body mass index (BMI) sits at **[rs9939609](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/snp/rs9939609)**, inside the **[FTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTO_gene)** gene, and wants to move fast on two fronts: treat FTO as the gene to chase for functional and drug target work, and fold the variant into a customer-facing obesity risk score. Before the team commits, they ask you for a short, evidence-based read.

**Your job:** write a consult memo that reaches a clear recommendation and defends it with the data. You are not writing a textbook summary. You are advising a decision, and you have to take a position.

This is the last lab and it works differently from Labs 1 to 6. There are no fill-in-the-blank starter chunks and no single right answer at the end. The only code given to you reads the files in. The analysis chunks name *what* to compute and leave the *how* entirely to you (and your AI friends). Labs 1 to 6 taught you the all the moves (allele frequencies, genomic coordinates and overlaps, variant annotation, GWAS summary statistics, public-data integration, expression). This one asks you to use them to advise a decision.

This document is both your instructions and your worksheet. Under each numbered heading there is a "What to do here" box, then space for your code and your writing. Work top to bottom. The data is included in `data/`. I encourage you to write the analysis code yourself, but you may use AI to help with or explain code so long as you disclose it at the end. **The interpretation and the recommendation must be your own words.**

## Before you start

- Render early and often. Submit the rendered `lab7_final.html`.
- Keep all data files in the `data/` folder next to this notebook.
- Every code chunk runs when you render. Each of the three analysis chunks ends in a `stop()` line that throws an error until you delete it, and errors print into the HTML instead of stopping the render, so **a chunk that still shows a red error block in your rendered HTML is not done**. A chunk left broken costs you those points even if the code beneath it is right.
- Complete the **AI disclosure** section at the end, including your audit of the AI brief. It is a scored part of this lab.

**Suggested length:** about 500-1,000 words of prose, not counting code, output, tables, plots.

**Grading.** This lab is worth 60 points (double a standard lab) and does not use the standard lab rubric. Most of the points are for what you conclude and how well your own numbers back it up. 

| Part | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Section 6: a clear position on both questions, with cautions tied to your numbers | 22 |
| Sections 2 to 4: correct analyses, and prose that interprets them | 19 |
| Section 5: verdicts, the ranking and why, two rewrites backed by a number | 16 |
| Renders cleanly, honest AI disclosure | 3 |

Everything is graded from the document you submit. After the due date we will walk through the case together in class, which is a debrief and is not graded.

### The data

All four files are **real downloads**, not teaching stand-ins, because you are drawing a real scientific conclusion from them. They were pulled once and staged so that graded work needs no internet.

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `data/lab7_fto_gwascat.csv` | Every association reported for this SNP in the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog: trait, risk allele, effect size, p-value, PMID. Left with its real rough edges (some rows report `?` for the allele, or no effect size). |
| `data/lab7_fto_af.csv` | Risk-allele (A) frequency by genetic-ancestry group, gnomAD genomes via Ensembl. |
| `data/lab7_fto_ccre.bed` | ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements within 20 kb of the SNP, from UCSC (hg38). |
| `data/lab7_fto_ai_brief.md` | An AI-written summary of this variant. You audit it in Section 5. |


# 4. Which gene does the variant act through?

::: {.callout-note}
## What to do here
Read `data/lab7_fto_ccre.bed` (ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements within 20 kb of the SNP, from UCSC). Work out two things: does the lead SNP position fall *inside* any of these candidate regulatory elements, and how many candidate elements sit in the window? Then reason in prose about the central question of the consult: the SNP sits in FTO, but is FTO necessarily the gene it acts on? Address the tag-versus-causal point (a GWAS lead SNP is usually a tag in linkage disequilibrium, not the proven functional variant) and the "nearest gene" trap, and say what kind of evidence would actually establish the causal gene.
:::

```{r read-ccre}

ccre
```

# 5. Fact-check the AI brief

## What to do here

Audit it. Fill in the table with a row per numbered claim: mark it **correct**, **overstated**, or **wrong**, and give a one-line reason grounded in *your own* results above or in course concepts. :::

```{r show-brief}
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
writeLines(readLines("data/lab7_fto_ai_brief.md"))
```

The brief makes five checkable claims:

1. Because the variant sits inside FTO, FTO must be the gene that causes the weight gain.
2. p ~ 4e-51 means the variant has a very large effect on BMI and explains a substantial fraction of obesity risk.
3. A person with two copies of the risk allele will become obese.
4. The risk allele is essentially absent outside Europeans, so the finding is mainly relevant to people of European ancestry.
5. Because the variant is intronic (not in a coding exon), it cannot have any functional consequence.

# 6. Your recommendation

::: {.callout-note}
## What to do here
This is the memo's point. In about 200 words, give the team your recommendation, grounded in Sections 2 to 4, on the two things they asked about: (a) should they treat FTO as the causal gene and prioritize it for functional and drug-target work, and (b) is rs9939609 a sound basis for a customer-facing obesity risk score? Take a clear position on each. Then list the specific cautions a data scientist must carry here, tied to your own numbers rather than generic boilerplate: the modest per-allele effect of a common variant, the tag-versus-causal problem and the nearest-gene trap, the ancestry differences in risk-allele frequency and what they do to a risk score's portability, and the fact that these frequencies and associations come from particular cohorts.
:::

> WRITE (~200 words): your recommendation on (a) and (b), and the case-specific cautions.
